newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel braces for Palestinian protests.
newsitem.headline: Israel braces for Palestinian protests.

text.p: Israeli security forces were braced on Wednesday to prevent violence in Jerusalem following Palestinian calls for protests against the opening of a tourist tunnel near the Temple Mount, a site holy to Jews and Moslems.
"We have pretty large forces, more forces are coming to Jerusalem and by the end of the week I hope we'll have calmed the situation," Aryeh Amit, police chief of Jerusalem, told Israel Radio.
He spoke after a day of unrest reminiscent of the Palestinian uprising that ended with the 1993 interim PLO-Israel peace deal reached under Israel's previous government.

Palestinians clashed with police on Tuesday after workmen, under cover of night and with a heavy police guard, punched a second entrance through a stone wall to a tourist tunnel beside Jerusalem's Temple Mount.

Police said they fired rubber bullets to disperse youths throwing stones and bottles and briefly evacuated Jewish worshippers from the Wailing Wall after stones were hurled from the Temple Mount above. Youths also set vehicles alight and police said 11 Arabs were arrested. No injuries were reported.

The Palestinian self-rule Authority cabinet, meeting in emergency session in Gaza late on Tuesday night, called for demonstrations throughout the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Jerusalem on Wednesday to protest against the tunnel.
"It will be tomorrow, between 12 p.m. to 2 p.m., an official strike with mass processions in all Palestinian areas," Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
A Palestinian cabinet statement said the Israeli move "proved to us that the Israeli leaders are not serious at all about the path of the peace process or respecting agreements".

The cabinet decision came shortly after the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) called on the U.N. Security Council to reverse Israel's action. The Higher Islamic Council has already called for a commercial strike in Jerusalem on Wednesday and demonstrations after noon prayers.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat called the tunnel a "crime" against the religious status quo in the disputed city, and a breach of the foundering Israeli-PLO peace accord.
The 488-metre-long (500-yard) tunnel, which exposes the Herodian foundations of the Wailing Wall, has been open for some time with only one entry and exit point in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City.
In London, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended opening the second entrance.

"(It is) a decision I am very proud that we are implementing," he told reporters. "Whoever has been in the Wailing Wall tunnel -- I was there a year ago -- could not help but feel the emotion to the depths of his soul...we are touching the rock of our existence," he said.
Israel's Channel Two television said on Tuesday that Netanyahu had promised a partner in his coalition government that 780 more homes for Jews will be built in the West Bank.

A Netanyahu spokesman in Israel said he could not comment on the report since his boss was out of the country. It was the latest in a flurry of reports and announcements on approvals to build thousands of housing units for Jews on the occupied lands.

Palestinians want final status peace talks to result in a state in the West Bank and Gaza with Arab East Jerusalem as capital. Netanyahu opposes both goals and these talks have yet to resume since he ousted Israel's previous centre-left government in May elections.
